sources.title: TCP vs UDP: Differences Between TCP & UDP Protocols
What Is the Difference Between TCP and UDP?
TCP vs UDP | 10 Key Differences Explained with Table & Examples

points.point: TCP is connection-oriented and uses a 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before data transfer.
UDP is connectionless; no handshake is performed before sending datagrams.
TCP provides reliable delivery via ACKs and automatic retransmission of lost segments.
UDP is best-effort; it does not guarantee delivery and does not retransmit.
TCP guarantees in-order delivery using sequence numbers.
UDP does not guarantee ordering of datagrams.
TCP uses a sliding window for flow control, throttling the sender to the receiver's capacity.
TCP implements congestion control (Reno, CUBIC, BBR) to protect the network.
UDP has no built-in congestion control; applications must handle it themselves.
TCP header is 20 bytes minimum, up to 60 bytes with options.
UDP header is a fixed 8 bytes.
TCP is slower due to handshake, ACKs, and retransmission overhead.
UDP is faster with minimal overhead, ideal for real-time applications.
TCP is used by HTTP/HTTPS, SSH, SMTP, FTP, and database protocols.
UDP is used by DNS, VoIP, video streaming, online gaming, NTP, DHCP, and QUIC/HTTP3.
